segments.t: In Gabriel's office, cautious agent Mathias questions Sofia about her meeting with singer Julien Dore. Mathias warns her to focus on acting alone, while Gabriel urges her to stay curious and hear Julien's offer. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Pourquoi tu parles avec Julien Doré?
Julien cherche une chanteuse pour son film.
Tu veux être chanteuse ou actrice?
Je suis actrice, bien sûr.
Oui, mais Sofia chante très bien aussi!
C'est une bonne occasion pour moi.
Non, c'est mauvais pour ton image.
Dans le cinéma, fais une seule chose.
Concentre-toi seulement sur le cinéma.
Mais non! Restons curieux et ouverts.
Écoutons la proposition de Julien d'abord.
D'accord, je vais parler avec Julien.
Let's explore the conversation line by line and unpack the French phrases.
Pourquoi tu parles avec Julien Doré?
'Why are you talking with Julien Dore?' Putting 'why' in front of plain 'you speak' is the relaxed spoken way to ask a 'why' question in French without flipping word order.
Julien cherche une chanteuse pour son film.
'Julien is looking for a singer for his film.' Remember that 'searches' already includes the 'for' idea in French, while actual 'for' only appears later before 'his film'.
Tu veux être chanteuse ou actrice?
'Do you want to be a singer or an actress?' Both professions stand bare without 'a' or 'an' after 'to be' in French, joined simply by 'or'.
Je suis actrice, bien sûr.
'I am an actress, of course.' Dropping 'an' before 'actress' treats a profession like an identity tag in French, sealed with an idiomatic 'well sure' for 'of course'.
Oui, mais Sofia chante très bien aussi!
'Yes, but Sofia sings very well too!' Tagging 'also' onto the end works just like 'too' in English, right after 'very well'.
C'est une bonne occasion pour moi.
'It is a good opportunity for me.' Watch the false friend: what looks like English 'occasion' usually means a 'chance' or 'opportunity' in French.
Non, c'est mauvais pour ton image.
'No, it is bad for your image.' Even though 'image' is female-gendered in French, 'your' switches to its '-on' form before a vowel sound so the words flow smoothly.
Dans le cinéma, fais une seule chose.
'In cinema, do just one thing.' Put ahead of 'thing', the word that means 'alone' shifts to 'single' or 'just one' in French, while 'cinema' keeps 'the'.
Concentre-toi seulement sur le cinéma.
'Focus only on cinema.' Literally 'concentrate yourself', this command tucks 'yourself' after a hyphen and pairs with 'on the cinema' in French.
Mais non! Restons curieux et ouverts.
'Of course not! Let us stay curious and open.' Opening with 'but no!' pushes back warmly in French, and the '-ons' ending builds 'let us stay' without any extra helper.
Écoutons la proposition de Julien d'abord.
'Let us listen to Julien's offer first.' In French, 'let us listen' already includes the 'to' idea, and possession is built as 'the offer of Julien'.
D'accord, je vais parler avec Julien.

'All right, I am going to talk with Julien.' Combining 'I go' with 'to speak' gives you a handy phrase in French for the near future, matching 'am going to talk'. Now let's listen to the whole dialogue once more to lock in what you have learned.

D'accord, je vais parler avec Julien.
Pragmatic Mathias urges Sofia to stick strictly to acting, while Gabriel encourages her to stay open to Julien Dore's musical film. See you next time!
À bientôt!
